newsitem.title: UK: Copper ends LME at lows, spreads also slacken.
newsitem.headline: Copper ends LME at lows, spreads also slacken.

text.p: Copper prices veered lower during late Thursday LME trading and with spread backwardations also softening the market notched up a poor technical close, ending at its lows, traders said.
Business was patchy, and once it became obvious that the market was not going to clear $2,215/2,200 - an area it has faltered at recently - declines started to accelerate.

Below $2,200, selling picked up, and the end of the kerb three months was trading at $2,179, down $29 from yesterday's kerb and just above a key long-term indicator. Cash/threes was at $150/155, some $15 softer.
Attention is being focussed on Friday's stocks data, and expectations are that there will be another build as metal is delivered into U.S. and Singapore stores.
Traders said that copper is still in the grips of a major battle between strong players on both sides of the market, which is likely to continue in the short-term.
A range is expected to prevail, but if prices clear $2,150 on the downside or $2,220 overhead there could be some savage price movements, they added.
Elsewhere, copper's woes impacted on most other metals, although the pace of trading was slow.
Aluminium attempted to push higher, with some traders citing good spot physical interest this week. However, the market was baulked by copper's trend.
"I see that copper is down, which means that aluminium will follow," one said.
Prices managed to stabilise above $1,520, and finished at $, a $ loss from the previous kerb.

Lead was content to hold just above $690, and closed at that level, up $2 from the previous kerb. Zinc drifted lower, however, even though there have been a clutch of mine closures and cutbacks recently. Last trade was at $1,065, down $4.
There was little movement in the nickel market throughout the session, with prices ending the day at $6,880 a tonne, a $65 loss from yesterday.
Tin also fell away, although the extent of the setback was fairly small with the market holding close to the $6,100 level. Last business was at $6,090, a $25 loss.
The alloy market was generally neglected, and closed at $1,360/65 a tonne, against Wednesday's level of $1,375.
